Dunkeld
dun-KELD
n. (the Perthshire cathedral town to which Columba's relics were brought from Iona about 849, making it the religious centre of the Scots)
Gaelic Dùn Chailleann, the fort of the Caledonians, from dùn, a fort, and the tribal name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Dunkeld is the small cathedral town where the Tay comes out of the Highlands into Strathmore, and for a time it was the chief religious place in Scotland. When Norse raiding made Iona untenable, Kenneth mac Alpin is recorded as having brought a part of Columba's relics to Dunkeld about 849 and built a church for them; the abbot of Dunkeld became one of the great men of the kingdom, and the primacy afterwards passed to St Andrews. The cathedral, built between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries, was gutted in 1560 when the Lords of the Congregation ordered the removal of its images and altars, and only the choir was later roofed again for the parish. In August 1689 a newly raised Cameronian regiment under William Cleland held the town against a far larger Jacobite force in a day of street fighting; Cleland was killed and the Jacobite advance was stopped. The dictionary records the removal of the relics from Iona as the plainest demonstration that a religion attached to objects must keep moving them, and names that as the opposite of the faith.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a relic as the remains of a saint; a shrine as a case for sacred things; to venerate as to regard with reverential respect; an image as a representation; and an idol as an object of worship besides God.

expand to see more

RELIC, n. That which remains; the body of a deceased person, or some part of it, preserved with veneration.

SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for sacred things; the tomb of a saint resorted to by devotees.

VENERATE, v.t. To regard with reverential respect; to reverence; to treat with the highest respect.

IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance.

IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

Act 17:29 — "Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device."

Jer 10:5 — "They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good."

1Jn 5:21 — "Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen."

Modern Corruption

Perthshire cathedral town to which part of Columba's relics were carried from Iona about 849 when Norse raiding made the island untenable, and whose cathedral was stripped of images in 1560.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the cult of relics, and Dunkeld exhibits its central absurdity better than any English shrine. A religion whose holiness is lodged in bones must evacuate them when the enemy comes. Columba's remains were divided and carried about, part going to Ireland and part up the Tay to a fort in Perthshire, and the primacy of the Scottish church followed the bones rather than any doctrine or office; when the bones moved, the centre moved. The commandment covers the whole class of such objects and forbids both their making and their use: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). John closes his epistle with the shortest possible application: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jn 5:21).

The second paragraph gives the reasoning, because the dictionary prefers to argue rather than merely to prohibit. Paul at Athens denies that the divine nature can be represented in material at all, since “we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device” (Act 17:29); if that holds of God it holds of anything made to carry access to Him. Jeremiah adds the mockery and with it a real comfort, that the object is inert in both directions, carried because it cannot walk, and so “Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good” (Jer 10:5). The dictionary notes that when the images and altars went out of Dunkeld cathedral in 1560 the choir was roofed for a congregation, and that a hundred and twenty-nine years later a regiment raised out of the covenanting societies died in its streets for a cause that needed no relics at all.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pesel (H6459), a graven image; Greek eidolon (G1497), an idol; Hebrew yatab (H3190), to do good.

expand to see more

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a carved or graven image; “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image”, Exodus 20:4.

Hebrew temunah (H8544) — a likeness, a form, a similitude; “or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above”, Exodus 20:4.

Greek theion (G2304)-sense of the Godhead in Paul's argument — “the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone”, Acts 17:29.

Hebrew yatab (H3190) — to be good, to do good; “neither also is it in them to do good”, Jeremiah 10:5.

Greek eidolon (G1497) — an image, an idol; “keep yourselves from idols”, 1 John 5:21.

Usage

"“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — relics carried up the Tay about 849."

"“the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone” (Act 17:29) — the argument, not merely the prohibition."

"“keep yourselves from idols” (1Jn 5:21) — the choir roofed for a congregation in 1560."
